title: CASE OF SEJDOVIC v. ITALY
conclusion: Violation of Art. 6;Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed;Non-pecuniary damage - finding of violation sufficient;Costs and expenses (national proceedings) - claim dismissed;Costs and expenses award - Convention proceedings
summary: In the case of Sejdovic v. Italy, the applicant, Mr. Cloce (or Kroce) Sejdovic, identified in the proceedings as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against Italy. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers, who often face barriers to justice, particularly when living in encampments and subject to negative stereotypes about evading legal processes. On 8 September 1992, following a fatal shooting at a Roma encampment in Rome, Mr. Sejdovic was identified by witnesses as the alleged perpetrator. Unable to locate him, Italian authorities declared him a fugitive and assigned him a lawyer, proceeding to try him in absentia. In July 1996, Mr. Sejdovic was convicted of manslaughter and illegal possession of a weapon, receiving a sentence of over twenty-one years, without ever having been notified of the charges or able to participate in his defence. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 6 (right to a fair trial), finding a violation due to the applicant’s conviction in absentia without effective notification or opportunity to defend himself. The Court considered the finding of a violation sufficient just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the importance of procedural safeguards and fair trial guarantees, especially for historically marginalised groups who are at heightened risk of exclusion from justice.
